transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

I guess… I’m here because I keep feeling like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. Especially at work. I’m a doctor, so people just sort of hand you this enormous responsibility, and lately I keep replaying small things—like tiny clinical imperfections, things other people might say are normal—and I turn them over and over until they feel like proof that I’m dangerous, like I shouldn’t be allowed to do this.

Sorry, that probably sounds dramatic. It’s just… even when nothing major happened, I can’t shake the feeling that it means something terrible about me.
Do you find that these thoughts about not being good enough or being dangerous come up repeatedly, even when there’s no clear reason for them?

Yes… yes, they do. It’s not always tied to something obvious. I’ll be driving home or trying to make dinner and suddenly I’m back on some small decision from work, some minor imperfection, and it starts feeling like evidence that I shouldn’t be trusted.

And I know people say, you know, doctors are supposed to review things and be careful—one of my attendings used to say good clinicians worry, the bad ones don’t—but this feels different. It turns into this… certainty almost, that I’m dangerous somehow, or that I don’t deserve the responsibility people give me.
Do these thoughts feel intrusive and unwanted, like they’re not quite your own, and do you try to suppress or neutralize them in some way?

I’m not sure, honestly. “Intrusive” is a word I hear patients use, and I know what it’s supposed to mean, but when it’s happening to me it doesn’t feel that clean.

It feels unwanted, yes, in the sense that I don’t want to be thinking about it. But it also feels like… like maybe I’m obligated to think about it, if that makes sense. Like if I stop turning it over, I’m being careless. I don’t know if that counts as suppressing or neutralizing.

Sometimes I try to distract myself, or I’ll go back through the situation in my head, but then I get pulled into the details—like one note I wrote last week, or the way someone phrased something in handover—and then I’m not really answering your question anymore. So… I guess I don’t know. I notice the thoughts, and I don’t like them, but I’m not sure what category they fit into.
When these thoughts come up, do you feel driven to do something—like checking, reviewing, or trying to fix the situation in your mind—to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

I… I don’t know if I’d say I’m “driven” exactly. I do go back over things in my head, but it’s hard to tell whether I’m trying to reduce anxiety or whether I’m just… thinking, like any careful doctor would.

Sometimes the line feels blurry. Like, in residency we were always told to double-check everything, and that becomes part of you. I had this senior once who could remember every lab value from rounds, and I used to think that was what competence looked like. So now when I replay something, I can tell myself it’s just diligence, but then it gets sort of sticky and I’m still there mentally long after it’s useful.

But whether I’m doing it to prevent something bad from happening… I’m not sure. I guess I haven’t thought of it that way.

When these thoughts come up, do you feel a strong need to do something—like re-reading notes, double-checking decisions, or going over the details again and again—to make sure everything is perfect or to ease your mind?

I’m not sure I can say it’s about making everything perfect. I mean, I do go back over details sometimes, but… medicine trains you to do that, doesn’t it? It’s hard to separate what’s reasonable from what’s me getting stuck.

Like, I’ll think about a note or a decision and then suddenly I’m remembering something an attending said years ago about how missed details are where mistakes happen, and then I’m not really checking anything concrete anymore, I’m just… circling it. But whether that eases my mind? Not really. Or maybe briefly. I don’t know.

I haven’t noticed a clear ritual, if that’s what you mean. It’s more like I get pulled into reviewing things, and then I lose track of whether it’s useful.

Do you ever find yourself repeatedly doing certain things—like re-reading notes, checking lab results multiple times, or going through decisions again and again in your head—not necessarily because you need to, but because it somehow feels necessary to avoid something bad happening or to calm the anxiety these thoughts bring up?

I’m not sure. I can think of times I look back at things, but I don’t know that I’ve noticed a pattern like… “if I don’t do this, something bad will happen.” It’s not that clear in my head.

And with labs and notes, I mean, everyone checks things twice sometimes. There was a whole culture around that where I trained—people would praise you for being meticulous, and then later it becomes hard to tell when meticulous is just meticulous versus when it’s… something else.

So I guess I don’t really know. I don’t think I’m doing some specific repeated thing to calm anxiety, at least not that I can point to. I just get caught thinking about it sometimes.

When you find yourself going over decisions or clinical details again and again, does it feel driven by a need to be certain that everything is right, or by a fear that something terrible might happen if you miss something?

I don’t know that I can separate those out cleanly. Sometimes it feels like wanting to be certain, but then I start thinking about what “certain” even means in clinical work, because there’s always ambiguity. I had an attending who used to say if you’re not uncomfortable, you’re not paying attention, which sounds wise until you’re lying awake thinking about some tiny detail from a chart.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I have a clear thought like, “something terrible will happen if I don’t check this.” It’s more that I get caught in the reviewing, and the more I review, the less settled it feels. I can’t really tell if it’s fear or just habit or… trying to be careful.

When you go over clinical details or decisions repeatedly in your mind, does it feel like you’re trying to reach a sense of certainty or 'just right' feeling, even if you can’t clearly explain why it feels important?

I don’t know. “Just right” is hard for me to pin down. I wouldn’t say I’m chasing that exact feeling, like a switch flips and suddenly it’s okay. It’s more… I start turning something over, and then I remember how in training there was always this emphasis on not missing the one small thing, you know? Like the whole case could hinge on some lab value buried in the chart.

But I’m not sure that means I’m trying to get certainty. Sometimes I think I’m just trying to feel less uneasy, and sometimes I’m not even sure what I’m trying to do anymore. It doesn’t really land in a clear way for me.
When you’re going over these clinical details or decisions in your mind, do you feel anxious or distressed while you’re doing it, like something might go wrong if you don’t get it 'right'?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxious in that exact way. Distressed, maybe, but it’s hard to tell if that’s because I think something will go wrong or because I’ve just been thinking about it too long.

Sometimes I’ll be going over something and then suddenly I’m remembering all these cases people talked about in training—like the cautionary tales, the “one missed detail” stories—and those kind of stick in your head. But I don’t know that I have a clear thought of, “If I don’t get this right, something bad will happen.” It’s more murky than that.

I guess I do feel unsettled while I’m doing it, but I can’t really say what I’m afraid of, if that makes sense.

Do you find yourself deliberately doing something—like re-reading notes, checking lab results, or going through decisions in your head in a specific way or for a certain amount of time—to try to reduce your distress or to prevent something bad from happening?

I don’t know that I do it in a structured way, if that’s what you mean. Like, I’m not counting how many times I read something or following a rule exactly.

I might look back at something, or think through it again, but it’s hard to say whether I’m doing it to prevent something bad or just because my mind gets stuck on it. In the hospital, everyone checks things, you know—labs, notes, sign-outs—and sometimes it’s just part of the culture of not wanting to be sloppy. Though I guess that doesn’t really answer your question.

So… no, I haven’t noticed a specific ritual or set amount of time. It’s more vague than that.
Have these thoughts about clinical decisions or details ever interfered with your work, relationships, or daily activities, or caused you significant distress even when you try to let them go?

Yeah… I think it has, though I keep wanting to qualify that because I’m still going in, I’m still showing up to clinic. It’s not like I’ve stopped working.

But the edges are fraying a bit. I’ve had to ask other people to help me with some of the non-urgent admin stuff, the things I normally would just handle. And then outside of work, I’ve been avoiding plans more. Someone will text about dinner or whatever, and I’ll just… I don’t trust that I’ll have the judgment or the energy to be decent company, I guess.

So yes, it’s started affecting how reliably I function at work, and I’m definitely less connected to people outside of it. Not in some dramatic way, but enough that I notice it.
Do you ever feel like these thoughts about your work or decisions keep coming back in a way that feels out of your control, even when you try not to think about them?

Yeah, they do come back. I mean, not like a pop-up window or something, but… I’ll be doing something else and suddenly I’m back on some tiny clinical detail from earlier, some wording in a note or a decision that probably wasn’t even the main issue.

And then it sort of turns into this bigger thing, like, “See, that’s proof you shouldn’t be trusted.” Which sounds extreme when I say it out loud. I know physicians are always talking about humility and double-checking, and in training they drill into you that confidence can be dangerous—one of my attendings used to say that constantly, actually, usually right before telling some horror story from residency.

But for me it’s not just learning from mistakes. It feels like I keep replaying small imperfections as if they mean I’m a dangerous doctor. Like I don’t deserve the trust patients or colleagues put in me. I try to move on from it, but it loops back.

Do you ever feel like you need to mentally go over something in a specific way, like repeating certain thoughts or following a mental routine, to try to feel better or prevent something bad from happening?

I don’t think so… not in that specific way. I mean, I do go back over things in my head, but it doesn’t feel like I have a set routine, like “repeat this phrase” or “review it three times” and then I’ll be safe.

It’s more messy than that. Like my brain just wanders back to it, and then I’m stuck there for a while. But I’m not deliberately doing a mental ritual, at least not that I’ve noticed.

I guess in medicine there’s so much internal rehearsal anyway—presenting patients, anticipating questions, thinking through differentials—and sometimes that blurs together. But no, I can’t point to a specific mental routine I feel compelled to follow.
Have these thoughts ever led you to avoid certain situations, responsibilities, or interactions because you were worried about not being able to manage them properly or being judged?

Yeah… I think so. Not in the sense that I’m refusing to do my job — I’m still going to clinic, still seeing patients. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

But I have been sort of sidestepping things. Like some of the non-urgent admin tasks, paperwork-type things I’d normally just knock out, I’ve asked other people for help with because I don’t feel like I can trust myself to handle everything cleanly right now. Which is embarrassing, because it’s not even the hard part of the job, you know?

And socially, yes. I’ve been avoiding plans. Someone will suggest dinner or meeting up, and I think, I’m going to be strange, or tired, or I won’t have the judgment to respond like a normal person. Then I just don’t go, or I let the text sit there too long.

So… yes, I guess I am avoiding some responsibilities and interactions. I’m still functioning, but less reliably than I’d like, and I feel pretty disconnected outside of work.
Do you feel more anxious or distressed if you try to stop yourself from going back over clinical details or decisions in your mind?

Yeah… I think I do. If I try to cut it off, it doesn’t really feel like relief, it feels like I’m being irresponsible somehow.

Like if I don’t go back over the note, or the decision, or whatever tiny clinical thing is bothering me, then I’m ignoring evidence that I’m not safe to trust. Which—sorry, that sounds dramatic. I know everyone misses wording here and there, and I’ve had colleagues tell me, “That’s just being conscientious,” but it doesn’t feel like that.

It feels more like… I’m here because I can’t shake this sense that I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. So when I stop reviewing it, the distress goes up, because part of me thinks I’m letting myself off the hook too easily.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you need to mentally go over something in a specific way, like repeating certain thoughts or following a mental routine, to try to feel better or prevent something bad from happening?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mental compulsions or rituals, such as repeating thoughts or following a mental routine to reduce distress or prevent harm. The provided symptom profile does not include compulsions or ritualized mental behaviors.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in that specific way. I mean, I do go back over things in my head, but it doesn’t feel like I have a set routine, like “repeat this phrase” or “review it three times” and then I’ll be safe.

It’s more messy than that. Like my brain just wanders back to it, and then I’m stuck there for a while. But I’m not deliberately doing a mental ritual, at least not that I’ve noticed.

I guess in medicine there’s so much internal rehearsal anyway—presenting patients, anticipating questions, thinking through differentials—and sometimes that blurs together. But no, I can’t point to a specific mental routine I feel compelled to follow.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to these thoughts, beyond what has already been disclosed.
doctor.question: Have these thoughts ever led you to avoid certain situations, responsibilities, or interactions because you were worried about not being able to manage them properly or being judged?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up to clinic, but I’ve had to ask for help with non-urgent administrative work and I avoid social plans because I don’t trust my judgment or energy. It has started to affect how reliably I function at work and how connected I am outside of it.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether the thoughts have led to avoidance of responsibilities or interactions and impaired functioning, which matches the functional impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. Not in the sense that I’m refusing to do my job — I’m still going to clinic, still seeing patients. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

But I have been sort of sidestepping things. Like some of the non-urgent admin tasks, paperwork-type things I’d normally just knock out, I’ve asked other people for help with because I don’t feel like I can trust myself to handle everything cleanly right now. Which is embarrassing, because it’s not even the hard part of the job, you know?

And socially, yes. I’ve been avoiding plans. Someone will suggest dinner or meeting up, and I think, I’m going to be strange, or tired, or I won’t have the judgment to respond like a normal person. Then I just don’t go, or I let the text sit there too long.

So… yes, I guess I am avoiding some responsibilities and interactions. I’m still functioning, but less reliably than I’d like, and I feel pretty disconnected outside of work.

inference.note: F42.8 was ruled out as the patient does not engage in repetitive mental acts or behaviors in response to obsessive thoughts in a way that meets criteria for OCD. The symptoms are more consistent with generalized anxiety and persistent doubting rather than a disorder classified under F42.8 (Other obsessive-compulsive disorders).

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences anxiety or distress specifically when prevented from reviewing or checking clinical details, which would support a compulsive behavior pattern consistent with OCD (F42.2).
doctor.question: Do you feel more anxious or distressed if you try to stop yourself from going back over clinical details or decisions in your mind?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I feel like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me, and I keep replaying small clinical imperfections as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor.
target_item.reason: The question is about distress when trying to stop mentally revisiting clinical details, which in this profile is tied to excessive guilt and replaying small clinical imperfections as proof of being a dangerous or unworthy doctor.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think I do. If I try to cut it off, it doesn’t really feel like relief, it feels like I’m being irresponsible somehow.

Like if I don’t go back over the note, or the decision, or whatever tiny clinical thing is bothering me, then I’m ignoring evidence that I’m not safe to trust. Which—sorry, that sounds dramatic. I know everyone misses wording here and there, and I’ve had colleagues tell me, “That’s just being conscientious,” but it doesn’t feel like that.

It feels more like… I’m here because I can’t shake this sense that I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. So when I stop reviewing it, the distress goes up, because part of me thinks I’m letting myself off the hook too easily.

opening_question.intent: Greet the patient and determine the primary reason for their visit
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts centered around perceived clinical imperfections and self-doubt regarding professional competence. These thoughts are accompanied by repetitive mental review of clinical decisions, which the patient engages in to alleviate distress or prevent perceived negative outcomes. The behavior is not better explained by generalized anxiety but rather fits the pattern of obsessive thoughts and compulsive mental acts seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The absence of a traumatic stressor rules out PTSD, and the presence of recurrent intrusive thoughts with mental rituals supports F42.2 over F43.10.
